utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, October 21st, 2008, and I welcome Ms. Biersay, Mr. Mundis, as well as their case manager. I also welcome Mr. Seselj. Let me first read a statement, and I would like Mr. Seselj to be extremely careful to listen to what I'm going to say. Last week, we dealt in public with the Prosecution's motion regarding contempt of court and dealing with the publication of one Mr. Seselj's books in which, according to Prosecution, protected witnesses were identified. The Prosecution, on several occasions, mentioned the accused, who had been involved in harassment or intimidation of Prosecution witnesses. This is an offence under Rule 77(A)(iii) of the Rules. These allegations by the Prosecution must, of course, be checked before any indictment be possibly drawn up against the accused or against any other person. When reading the written submissions made by the Prosecution, as a judge, I wondered whether I should not withdraw myself under Rule 15(A) of the Rules of Procedure regarding contempt of court procedures. Indeed, it seems to me very obvious that if the allegations made by the Prosecution end up being confirmed through an investigation, the question of the motivation that made the accused do this must best be answered. Why would the accused Seselj try to threaten or intimidate witnesses? The only reason could be to escape his criminal responsibility in our case. This being said, I believe that I would never be able to serenely try the accused Seselj in the case at hand if I am fully convinced that he was involved in threatening and harassing witnesses, because if that was the case, I might have a bias regarding his criminal liability in the main case that I am trying. This potential connection between the main case and the marginal cases dealing with contempt of court, but involving the same accused, i.e., Mr. Seselj, make it impossible for me to be in charge of the contempt of court cases. This is why I have informed the President of the Tribunal of my personal decision, which is to withdraw myself from any case dealing with contempt of court, and this is why I asked the President of this Tribunal to appoint another Judge that would be sitting on these cases to replace me. I must say that up until now, my fellow Judges, Judges Harhoff and Lattanzi, have not had the same approach so far. So, on top of this withdrawal, as the President of the Trial Chamber and heading the proceedings of this Trial Chamber according to Article 14 of the Statute, I asked the President of the Tribunal to appoint another Trial Chamber that would be in charge of dealing with the contempt of court submissions, because managing in parallel two cases --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... if two Judges of the Trial Chamber are dealing with two cases, this might slow down the trying of this case, which must be speedy according to Rule 20 of the Statute. The investigations which are to be carried out in respect with the contempt of court proceedings might take months if they are done competently and seriously. Furthermore, should people eventually be indicted and tried in this respect, according to me there is a serious risk that the present case be paralysed. Insofar that this Tribunal has 16 permanent Judges and 14 ad litem Judges, setting up an ad hoc Trial Chamber for these contempt of court proceedings would be no problem. The accused is entitled, according to Article 21 of the Statute, to be -- to a speedy trial. He's entitled to a speedy trial. This is written in the Statute and to be judged without delay. Since the accused has been jailed for six years now, I believe that there is undue delay so far. Managing new motions and dealing with new motions that would further increase the delay would increase this delay. This is why I asked the President of this Tribunal to appoint a new Trial Chamber. To sum things up, as far as I'm concerned, I withdrew myself from all contempt of court proceedings; and in order to make sure that the present case is speedy, I asked the President to please set up and appoint a new Trial Chamber to deal with these contempt of court proceedings. This Trial Chamber, of course, will be able, without undue delay, to try this case. The Prosecution still has about 40 hours to present its case and its witnesses. There is no reason to paralyse this present case with marginal procedures. In a nutshell, Mr. Seselj, this is what I wanted to tell you: This decision was difficult to make, but I believe that in the interests of justice and in the interests of your present case, I should not be involved in managing other marginal cases that might lead to undue delay in your present case. We have been sitting in court for more than a year now, and you have been awaiting trial for six years altogether, which is why I have asked the President to make a decision on my withdrawal, on the one hand, and also on the appointment of a new Trial Chamber that would deal with the contempt of court proceedings. If you have anything to say, please take the floor; otherwise, we will move to other topics.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that your decision, from the legal aspect, is quite in order because it is quite obvious that the Prosecution is using political methods in settling accounts with me because of its incompetence to bring this trial to an end by legal and lawful means as envisaged by the Statute. I'd like to remind you that on a number of occasions, the representatives of the OTP publicly acknowledged that they had planned that 90 per cent of the witnesses be heard under 92 ter; and for fours year, yes, four years, a full four years, they endeavoured to impose Defence counsel on me, a counsel of their choice, so that this trial should be conducted by bypassing me so that I should have no possibility for defending myself. Now, since it didn't succeed in doing that, and as I do have the means of defending myself, although I'm not satisfied with the resources and the circumstances and conditions because they're putting obstacles in my way all the time, the Prosecution doesn't know how to get out of this impasse situation. Now they're launching a campaign against me, stating I'm intimidating witnesses. I have never intimidated a single witness. I have not exerted any pressure or brought coercion to bear against witnesses. For years, I didn't even know the names of the witnesses; and, last year, I launched a process for respect of the trial on the basis of people who the Prosecution heard, but never agreed to -- people who never agreed to be Prosecution witnesses, starting with Jovo Ostojic and many others. I'm sure you remember all their names. Now, when I stated that publicly, when I informed the public of that, then they came at me from all sides, people from the Prosecution list, stating that they had been manipulated, that they had been intimidated and had to sign something that was not their statement. So that is the essence of it. Now, in addition to this (redacted), there is a great deal of mistification on the basis of this book, and it is a report that my associates compiled for me as an attachment for my last complaint against the indictment. You know the text was rather a lengthy one, about 300 pages, and you ordered that it should not be translated into English. I said that it should be printed and published but that the names be thrown out and that code names be used, the codes used by the Prosecution; and in that book, you'll see those codes. Now, the fact that somebody who is clever and intelligent can draw their own conclusions as to who the person is, well, what do I care about that? Now, the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Mr. Mundis is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Again, we would very vigorously, respectfully, request the Trial Chamber to caution Mr. Seselj with respect to any comments he makes about this book, in light of the fact that we have indicated in this courtroom before that we have filed a contempt motion concerning this book; and to the extent Mr. Seselj, in court, talks about this book, and how it was produced, and who produced it, and under what circumstances and what were done, those statements very well might be incriminatory, and we would vigorously asked that he be cautioned not to discuss that, or at least warned that anything he says concerning that could be used against him in subsequent proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, yes, refrain from talking about the content of this book, please. You already mentioned all this last week. We all know what you want to say, we all know what you said, so do not talk about the content of the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am proud of that book. That book was compiled absolutely pursuant to my strict instructions, instructions given from The Hague here to my associates; and everything that that book contains, I stand by the contents. My associates were just my extended arm, so to speak, in compiling that book. Now, you can't make me afraid and intimidate me through saying that I'll be held in contempt of court in this trial, where I might be sent to jail for years, for life. Now they say that I might get seven years for contempt of court. Why should I care about that? I will take great satisfaction in taking part in the proceedings and in showing exactly how things stand. So you can't intimidate me in that way or instill fear in me. Everything I stated, I stand by it. I have never given up on a single word uttered by me, and everything I did state and utter through my lifetime, if possible, I made public and published in my books, and I'm proud of that, too. So there's no need for you to discuss that matter at all. Now, what is the essence of the matter here, the crux of the matter? The Prosecution wants to buy time, and it is doing its utmost to prolong these proceedings. Last week, for instance, we lost one day because they didn't have any witnesses. This week, quite obviously, we're going to lose another day, because when we finish with this expert witness, we have a 92 ter witness and then nothing after that. So we've lost a month because they asked that the proceedings be interrupted until their request for me to be assigned counsel be decided on. So far, we've heard 43 Prosecution witnesses, and they experience -- the Prosecution experienced a fiasco with all those witnesses. They still have nothing, no straw to catch on to, to support their thesis from the indictment. They have absolutely nothing in their hands yet, and the whole public can see that, and especially you as members of the Trial Chamber, because you were present during the secret sessions here as well. Now they're doing everything they can to get themselves out of the situation, and there's just one way out for the Prosecution, and that is total and full capitulation. The sooner they capitulate, the better for them. They'll save face that way. They are faced with capitulation, and they want to prevent their own capitulation by opening some auxiliary fronts. Now, if I am capable of being victorious and winning over them in the main front, I certainly will be able to deal with the auxiliary fronts. Judges, in this Tribunal, there were cases where Prosecution witnesses were even killed, where they were abducted. In the Milosevic trial, for instance, one witness's son and daughter were seized and liquidated. Listen carefully. This was a Defence witness. Now, in this trial, not a hair on any of the witnesses' heads was dealt adversely with. It was only a moral contempt, that is, when a witness was found lying and when one witness testified in one way. It was just moral condemnation, and moral condemnation is not tantamount to pressure exerted upon the witness or intimidation. Each one of us can be exposed to moral condemnation, members of the Trial Chamber, members of the Prosecution, and I, myself, if we do something which is morally reprehensible. Everything that is against the law and unlawful is also, in the broader sense of the word, morally untenable and deserves moral condemnation. I consider that your decision is very correct. Nothing must stand in the way of this trial, even if I'm alone and without any associates or anything. I still take part in this trial and I'm ready to do so, and the Prosecution must be ready to do so. As soon as contempt of court proceedings are launched, then there are sessions outside -- being held outside the main trial proceedings. We can have different shifts. This can be during different shifts, at night, during the weekend. I'm not interested when these extra sessions take place, but I do insist that any auxiliary proceedings do not impede the normal development of this trial and these proceedings, because all reasonable deadlines for wrapping up the trial have expired a long time ago, all reasonable deadlines. We are now entering into the unreasonable realm of deadlines, and there is no precedent for anything like this in the civilised world. Now, what can the Prosecution prove? It cannot prove a thing. They can't find anybody whom I intimidated and exerted pressure upon. That kind of person just does not exist. They cannot prove that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, let me cut you off here. As I told you, I am not involved in the contempt of court proceedings, so I did not have any competence to be listening to all this. I wanted to inform you of my personal decision. I want you to have an expeditious trial in the main case. That is my main concern, and I felt that I could not do this while trying you for a contempt of court proceeding. So I want to focus only on your main case and only on this one. I'm still awaiting the decision from the President as to whether another Trial Chamber will be appointed. So either the President believes that my two fellow Judges can sit on that Bench and will appoint another Judge, and this new Bench will deal with the contempt of court proceeding as they wish. I want to remain only in charge of the main case. Now, regarding this main case, now we must move into private session because I must ask the Prosecutor about an important topic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me remind you, Ms. Biersay, that you'll have half an hour to put questions to the witness, to introduce her expert report. Mr. Seselj will have two hours to conduct his cross-examination of the witness. The Judges will have questions, of course; and, if necessary, you will be entitled to put additional questions. You were granted one hour to do so, if it appears necessary; but if the cross-examination and the Judges' questions are sufficiently comprehensive, this additional time won't be necessary. But we'll see how things stand as we go along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Can you please give me your first name, last name, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Ewa Tabeau; date of birth, 26th of April, 1958.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a demographer in the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have had the opportunity to hear you testify in other cases. I know that you've already testified in other cases. Could you please give us the list of all the trials you testified in as an expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This list is attached as part of my curriculum vitae submitted with other materials in this case. I will mention a number of cases. Most recently, I testified in Lukic and Lukic case, in the Dragomir Milosevic case, I testified in the Prlic case, Slobodan Milosevic case, General Galic. I testified in Popovic case, in Simic et al, and Vasiljevic. I think that would be probably more or less complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may be seated. Very well. You've said so yourself, you've testified in this Tribunal on several occasions. You're probably the expert witness who has testified the most in this Tribunal, so what I'm going to say won't come as a surprise to you. You know that you are going to first answer questions put to you by Ms. Biersay. Afterwards, Mr. Seselj, who is the accused in this case, will put questions to you as part of the cross-examination. The three Judges sitting in front of you may also ask you questions with respect to the contents of your report. This is what I wanted to tell you by way of an introduction. Please try to be extremely accurate and specific when you answer questions. If a question is not clear enough to you, do not hesitate to ask the person, even if it's a Judge, to rephrase the question. We have breaks every 90 minutes, but if at any time you want us to stop for whatever reason, do not hesitate to make that request to us. You have made the solemn declaration and you know that your testimony is likely to continue tomorrow. Let me remind you that you are a witness in the service of justice. In other words, you're not supposed, from now on, to have any contacts with the OTP, with your superiors at the OTP. If you have to go back to your office, remain in your office, but avoid any contacts with your colleagues at the OTP in order to try to avoid any type of interference between you, as a witness, and the Prosecution. But you know that as well as I do, you've probably been warned about that in the past, and the Trial Chamber fully trusts you in that respect. Ms. Biersay, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Given the Court's 15 October 2008 decision qualifying Dr. Tabeau as an expert with respect to her Hrtkovci report, I won't be covering a tremendous amount of her background.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: But what I would like to ask you, Dr. Tabeau: Could you please tell us the highest degree that you hold and from what institution you obtained that degree?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have a Ph.D. in mathematical demography. I obtained this degree from the Warsaw School of Economics in Poland, in Warsaw [Realtime transcript read in error "Moscow"].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: For how long have you been employed with the OTP demography unit?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have been here since September 2000, which is approximately eight years.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you briefly describe your general duties in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My unit is responsible for providing statistics --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Tabeau. I heard that you received your diploma in Warsaw, but here in the transcript we see "Moscow." So where did you obtain your diploma, your degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Warsaw, in Poland, not in Moscow. I've never been to Moscow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, very well. That's line 9, page 23 of the transcript. "Warsaw" should be put here instead of "Moscow."

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described before that a copy of your CV was attached to the report that you produced in this case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that annex B to the report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you also prepare a more updated version of your CV?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It is a brief version. The latest achievements mainly are included.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that in your binder as 2859B, 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to the report that you produced in this case. That report was dated 29 June of 2006; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the title is "Out-migration of Croats and other Non-Serbs form village of Hrtkovci in Vojvodina in 1992"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Just for ease of reference, I'll be referring to it as either your report or the Hrtkovci report, just so you can follow me when I ask those questions. I'd like to direct your attention, it should be the first document in your binder, which is 65 ter 2859.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that the report that you produced for this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now direct your attention to the methodology, the sources, and approach that you used in the compilation of your report for this case. How do the methodology, sources, and approach used to compile this report compare with those used in other cases in which you have testified as an expert?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: They are fully consistent with all other sources, the reports, and methodology and sources are used in these reports; full consistency.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Based on your professional training and experience, are those methodologies, sources, and approach consistent with the acceptable standards used within the field of armed conflict demography?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, of course, and more broadly with statistics, the approach used in statistics.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention now to annex A of your report, what does annex A represent?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is a list of persons, the number of these persons is 722, that are known to me as having left Hrtkovci in relation to the events in May-August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What time period does that annex cover?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Basically, it is the time around the summer of 1992, around the period from May to August 1992, but there are also records --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, let me interrupt you immediately. I'm listening to you with a great deal of interest, and I have a question with respect to the list. You are telling us that it is a list of persons that left the village between May and August 1992, but please have a look at the first name on the list, "Akrap." You have a column here called "Departure," and I see here that he left on the 15th of December. Isn't there a problem here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is no problem. This is what I was just going to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please explain away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The list is titled "Persons who left Hrtkovci in relation to the events in May to August 1992," but the list should be seen more broadly. So it is not only the departures in this exact period from May to August 1992. These are the departures from Hrtkovci mainly in this period, but including as well departures earlier in this year and later in this year. And in addition to this, there are 13 individuals who left -- listed here in annex A who left Hrtkovci in the first half of 1993. So, once again, this list should be seen as more broadly than just the period from May to August 1992. It is general departures related to the events during this period, but the departures are the majority of them, and the majority of them would be May to August 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should we then conclude that some departures occurred before May 1992, but these departures were caused by the events that took place between May and August? Is it what you are trying to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. This is not what I'm trying to tell Your Honours. Well, I think I said clearly this is a broader list. Of course, the departures starting from May and later most certainly are, in the first place, related to the events in the beginning of May and what was happening later; but as far as I know, the situation in this area was already affected by the general situation in the former Yugoslavia and by the conflict in Croatia, which started, of course, in 1991. So it is not that the departures from Hrtkovci in this period were exclusively related to certain events in May. I think it was a general situation that had some impact on these departures as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I'm not mistaken, if I understand you well, it might be that someone who leaves this village in May would be leaving not because what had happened in May, maybe even Mr. Seselj's speech on May 6th, but for other reasons that may have to do, as you said, with the general situation prevailing at the time. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my report, I didn't study the causes, in terms of quantification of these factors, so I can't say what were the causes of these departures. However, I studied the timing of these departures, and the timing is shown, first of all, in long-term perspective, since 1949 until the year 2000, which is long enough to see all kinds of patterns in the departures. On the other hand, I also show -- I'm showing that I'm in the year 1992; and from this pattern, time pattern, you see again certain irregularities, which I will talk about later. So I didn't study the causes, but certain conclusions can be drawn about underlying determinants of this migration from the analysis of the timing that I present in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was asking these questions, Madam Witness, to be specific, because we have seen a number of witnesses in this courtroom who came to testify. We heard them and we saw documents also, and thanks to this we know that a number of Croats left this village before May 1992. We know that some of them, a few dozens, left to join the Croatian National Guard, so these were voluntary departures. I'm just wondering whether they are involved in your statistics, these voluntary departures.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I'm unable, in my report, to distinguish between voluntary and involuntary departures, as I didn't study the causes of these departures. Obviously, certain sources that I used in my report can be seen most definitely as involuntary departures. That would be the list of refugees registered in Croatia, refugees from Hrtkovci; and these persons had a legal status of a refugee, that is, a person who didn't leave voluntarily. That is certain. And, well, there is another list I'm using as a source. The list is called "Expelled persons From Hrtkovci." Of course, these persons don't have the legal status of refugees or internally expelled person, but they are called expelled, and, probably, there are good reasons for this, that they are called like that. So, even though I didn't study the causes, I believe the majority of these departures are involuntary departures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to tab number 2859A, is that an amended version of the annex A to your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you briefly describe in what way it was amended?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is basically the same list, but at some point we saw a formatting mistake in the date of birth. Some dates were reported with the year of birth, beginning with a "9" or "8" or "5." It would be, for instance, "9932," so obviously something went wrong in data processing of the; and, indeed, there was a formatting problem during the data processing. The number of date of birth originally attached with the report were wrong and were correctly recently. This is the correct version of the annex A.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that in your original annex A, all years should have been listed as starting with the number "1"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. Definitely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, the Prosecution moves for the admission of 65 ter numbers 2859, which is the original report with the original annex A and B. We would also move for the admission of 65 ter number 2859A, which is the amended annex A; as well as 65 ter number 2859B, which is the updated CV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me conduct with my colleagues, but, first, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that before that, the expert should tell us who compiled this list. It is attached to the expert report, it is an annex, but did the expert compile it or was it somebody else who compiled it beforehand and the expert just took it over?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, this list on annex A, could you please tell us whether you compiled it yourself or was it done by someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This report was made in my unit, including the list in annex A. I had assistance from two members of the Demographic Unit. This is two colleagues of mine, Arve Hetland and Neda Loncaric. I think we compiled the list together, in the sense that each of us did a part of the work. So it is not that one single person compiled the entire list. The list is not taken from any other source. It is a list resulting from a combining of a number of underlying sources, and I think I should list the sources right now. One of them is the list of refugees I just mentioned a few minutes ago. This list was obtained from the Croat authorities from Croatia. It is a list of 116 individuals. Secondly, we used for this list the parish records from Hrtkovci. From these sources, the names were taken for which requests for certificates of christening and marriage were marked, written down in the parish books. And the third source was the list of expelled persons from Hrtkovci, the 280 families representing 805 persons, from a book by Marko Kljajic about these issues. But basically the list of 280 families comes from the same sources, the parish records. It is the Catholic Church in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will give an MFI number so far; and after Mr. Seselj's cross-examination, we will either give a final number or not. Mr. Registrar, could we have MFI numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. 65 ter number 2859, which is the expert report, will be MFI P565; 65 ter number 2859A, which is the amended annex A, will be Exhibit -- will be MFI P566; and 65 ter number 2859B, which is the updated CV, will be MFI P567.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In your report, Dr. Tabeau, do you discuss exactly how annex A was created by merging these sources?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes. There is a detailed description of how the matching was done, how the sources were assessed, whether there were duplicates or not. Of course, duplicates, a few duplicates, were found and eliminated. The overlapping records were excluded. So the list represents a merge of three groups of sources. In these three groups, we have five specific sources, and it's a list that is compiled in my unit. It's not coming from an external source.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I may now direct your attention to the tab marked 4100 in your binder, that is 65 ter number 4100, and it would be after the series 2859. Is that 65 ter number 4100 one of the sources used in compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is. This is the so-called refugee table. This list represents the refugees from the village of Hrtkovci registered in the Croatian system of internally-displaced persons and refugees. This list represents the persons who were still in this system as of mid-2005, so many years after the events of 1992. There are 116 persons on this list. All of them are listed as arriving in Croatia from Hrtkovci, most of them in 1992, 113, and the remaining 13 in 1993. I have even made a chart showing the time distribution of the arrivals based on this list, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'll stop you for one minute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, the Prosecution moves for admission of 65 ter number 4100, which is referred to in the report as the refugees table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Here, again, we'll give an MFI number. Mr. Seselj first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Along with this document, we have no markings of it being official. All we have is a table, nothing more than that to say that it is official. Whose document is this? Should we trust the expert at her word? I don't believe anything she says. She says that this is a document of the Croatian authorities. Where can that be seen? All we have here is a table without any other markings to tell us that it is an official document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This had not escaped me. We'll give it an MFI number anyway. Madam Witness, this table, 4100, you're telling us that you obtained these figures from the Croatian authorities. I assume that the OTP sent an official letter to the Croatian authorities, requesting from them the list of all people who had been registered in Croatia in 1992 as coming either from Serbia or from the village of Hrtkovci; and I guess in their return mail, a few months later, the authorities gave you that list. Now, this chart that we have, this table that we have here, is it the table that you obtained from the authorities or did you reformat this table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the original table as obtained from the authorities. It's not reformatted. But you are right, Your Honour, indeed, we made an official RFA to the government of Croatia sometime in, as far as I remember, in 2005; and in response to this RFA, we received, among other things, this list. There is a reference to the RFA in my report on the first page of section 1. As far as I remember, the number of this RFA is referred to, which I can show now. I hope that the copy is already disclosed. If not, I will, of course, do this immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I trust you on this. I have no element whatsoever that would make me -- lead me to think that things did not happen as you are saying. So you obtained this document from the Croatian authorities. Now, did you take a look as to the -- did you take a look at the procedure that was happening in Croatia? When somebody arrived, what did this person have to do? What documents did this person have to produce to prove that this person was Croatian? It could be a person from Tahiti or a person from Albania or whatever, you know, that might want to take advantage of the system. So what exactly was the procedure used at the time in Croatia? Who was in charge of the records, of the data? Did you take a look to know what was going on at the time, what ministry was involved, what department was involved? Did you investigate into this? I'm sure you did, but could you shed some light on this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We've been interested in the Croatia registration of internally displaced persons and refugees for a long time, this office. We did already some investigations and visits to this group of people in Croatia already in 2003 for the needs of the Slobodan Milosevic trial then. It's an important source of information. It's a system that was established in Croatia initially by the UNHCR together with the authorities from the government of Croatia. This system is -- was implemented as well in other countries of the former Yugoslavia, in Bosnia, of course, in Serbia as well. It's a standard procedure based on what an international organisation, renowned international organisation, UNHCR, brought into these countries. This system is based on a lot of experience from countries all over the world. There was a ministry -- there is a ministry in Croatia who is taking care of the system; and at some point, it was a ministry called, I think, the Ministry of Labour, and many other things, a very long name which I can't recall from my head, but I have the full name in the documentation. I visited this group of people. I had the opportunity to talk to them about how the information is received, how the document is stored, and how the document is -- how the documents are computerised. I had the opportunity to see the archive in which individual files of IDPs and refugees are kept. So, indeed, there is a requirement to provide certain documents that would allow the entry into the system; and based on these documents and on the statements from individuals applying for being registered, a decision is made, official decision, by appropriate authorities. In the case of Hrtkovci, normally, say, it is basic documents that are required related to the birth certificate and record of place of residence, and a statement or documents related to the fact whether or not a person was persecuted for whatever reasons. It's important to have a complete picture in order to make this legal decision of assigning the status of an IDP or a refugee to an individual. This decision, of course, has certain financial implications. People who have the status of IDPs and refugees are entitled to certain financial compensations. The authorities registering these people help them to find accommodation and et cetera. In the case of Hrtkovci, the situation was complicated because it was, for many of these people, obviously difficult to obtain regular birth certificates and records of their residence from official authorities in Vojvodina. It is not that I was there in Croatia and in 2005 when the data were provided to us on these refugees from Hrtkovci, but I know that instead of birth certificates and records of residents, other documents were accepted, and these documents were the documents provided by the Catholic Church in Hrtkovci. I'm speaking of parish records related to the christening, and, of course, based on christening, date of birth automatically become -- became available. There is also another type of record, the request for the certificate of marriage. That is another type of alternative document that was accepted by the Croatian authorities at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So the office of refugees and displaced persons in Croatia, in Zagreb, set up this document, which is listed as 4100. This comes from the Croatian authorities. I think you added one detail. You said 1992 and 1993. Were they computerised at the time they obtained all these elements, and they were able to computerise all these elements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a very good question, Your Honour. In 1992 and 1993 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All my questions are excellent; I hope so, anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry for my comment, then. Right. It's important to realise that at that time, there was no electronic system, 1992-1993. It was the time when the system was just being started; therefore, these first individuals were not available in records, electronic records from a computer system. There are, however, files of these individuals kept by the Croatian authorities; and, of course, it would be a matter of searching through the archives in order to identify the individual files. Later, in 1994, there was a survey in which a record was taken and computerised of all then-persons having the status of IDPs and refugees, and this is the first wave of data that is electronically available. But this registration system is a dynamic system, so whenever a decision is made to assign the status of an IDP or a refugee, then a new person enters the system and there is a new record. However, if the person is settled down somewhere there in Croatia, then the person loses the status of an IDP or a refugee and it's out of the system. So this explains why, by 2005, only 116 records from Hrtkovci are there in the electronic data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is very important. Thank you. This document that we have here, this document 4100, when exactly was it compiled by the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately by mid-2005. That is the time shortly afterwards, I assume, our RFA was submitted to the Croatian government. So, in response to this RFA, this data was extracted from the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Second important element which you mentioned, and I need you to confirm it: So when someone was granted the status of IDP or refugee and then would change status, was becoming Croatian, had a Croatian passport or left for somewhere else abroad, this person was taken out of the file. Is that it? You said that it was taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I said, and that is the dynamic nature of the system. It changes all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This list that was compiled in 2005, could you tell us whether it only deals with the people who remained IDP or refugees? In this list, can you tell us whether that there are no people who would have arrived, for example, in June 1992, who obtained the IDP status, and then say, "Well, now, three months from this, I'm going to Canada. I no longer want to be a refugee or an IDP, found another solution for my life" so they are no longer on the list; or some that say, "I want to return to Serbia," because we have seen people who return to Serbia, actually. So please confirm that this 2005 list, whether it is a comprehensive list with everyone or whether it's a list where we only have those who are still IDP or refugees in 2005 and not those who changed status between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is a list of actually exclusively refugees, because these are people from outside Croatia, from Hrtkovci, who ended in Croatia, who still have the status of a refugee in 2005. So, basically, they are still there in Croatia and didn't acquire a permanent residence in Croatia or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which means that a person, refugee, who would have arrived in Zagreb in June 1992, who obtained the status of refugee and who decided a few months later to move abroad, to Canada, and told that to the authorities, would not be in that list, in this 2005 list; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is how it works, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. That's what I understood. It goes without saying, but it's good to say it. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an arbitrary explanation given by the alleged expert. You can't see that anywhere from this document. The expert now says, without never having said that before, that this is the situation dating back to 2005 and that these individuals had the status of refugees in 2005. We have no prove in evidence showing us that they ever enjoyed the status of refugees. I don't suppose the documents from 1992 and 1993 have been destroyed. I assume that was accessible to the Croatian statistics. So this is being planted on us here, which was -- this was compiled just for the purposes of these proceedings, of this trial. They're trying to pull a fast one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I know you are very competent, but our expert is also extremely competent, notably in demographics and migration flows. So she told us that this file was matched and cross-matched with other sources. She did not just use that document -- You did not just use this document, this 2005 document, to reach your conclusions; right, Mrs. Tabeau? You tried to match this and cross-match this with other sources, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's right, I did. Moreover, I would like to add, I have been working with data on IDPs and refugees for a long time now. It's been Croatia data, it's been the Bosnian data from the conflict in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do have a lot of expertise in how these data is compiled, and how the data is changing over time, and what kind of decisions and how they are made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm sure that we will come back to this later on, but it's time for a break. Our Registrar is also someone that takes care of everything. He is going to give me an MFI number for the 4100 document. Mr. Registrar, could you please give me that MFI number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI P568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Ms. Biersay, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now direct your attention to what's in your binder as 65 ter number 2154A, which should be right after 65 ter number 4100; and at this time, I'd just like to briefly touch upon the last two sources in the next two tabs before you. In looking at 65 ter number 2154A, is that one of the sources that you used for the compilation of your report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: That would be the top 02154A?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, that is one of the remaining sources. It's the list of expelled persons from Hrtkovci. There are 280 families on this list, and the entire list represents 805 persons; and in addition to the list, there is a cover letter that was associated and presented together with the list in the book by Marko Kljajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honours, we would move for the admission of 65 ter number 2154A, which is an extract from a book which is 65 ter number 2154, but we're simply asking for the admission --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- of the extract at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give you the floor later on, Mr. Seselj. Just one point of clarification with the Prosecutor. I've had a look at the list and at the cover letter. If I understand correctly, you asked Mr. Marko Kljajic to send you that list. So how did it all happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't ask Marko Kljajic to send me the list. I have the book by Marko Kljajic titled "How My People Were Dying" in my office; and in this book, well, we saw this list and the letter. And, on the other hand, this list was as well provided to me as part of the RFA that we sent to the Croatian authorities with our request for information related to out-migration from Hrtkovci, 1992. So in this response received by me 2005, this list was attached, the letter wasn't, but identified the same list in the book by Marko Kljajic, and then the cover letter is there with the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is so impudent that it goes beyond words. This is not an accompanying letter along with a list. This is a letter that Ciril Kos, bishop, sent to the Serbian patriarch, Pavle, on the 6th of July, 1992. That letter has nothing whatsoever to do with the list. It just happens to be in the book on page 45, and the list starts on page 46. I believe that it would be best if the entire book would be admitted into evidence so that this kind of deceit would not take place in the future. However, this is total impudence that an alleged expert is offering this as a letter. You can see it on the basis of the content for yourselves, because the bishop, the Catholic bishop, heard there were persecutions. He's writing to the Serbian patriarch, but he's not sending a list; and at the time, he's not aware of any list. The list was made subsequently by Marko Kljajic as he manipulated information from the bishop's office --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Parish priest's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, I'm trying to understand what this letter is related to. Apparently, Ciril Kos is writing to the patriarch who is in Belgrade, but this letter, at first sight, does not seem to be related to the list. How do you establish a link between this letter and the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is a link, and this was a seminar of priests that took place around July 2000 -- 1992, at which issues related to the population in the area of not only Hrtkovci but the broader region in this part of Vojvodina were discussed. And at this seminar, I believe the seminar is summarised in the same book by Marko Kljajic, and this letter and the list are part of the materials presented just after the summary of the seminar. So it's -- well, I can't make another link; but just by looking and studying these materials, I can associate with them. Whether this is a manipulation, as Mr. Seselj called it, I would totally disagree, because these three documents are fully consistent with each other. There is the seminar report, at which these kind of issues are explicitly mentioned of the population being simply forcibly displaced from Hrtkovci; the letter; and the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you, Witness. I'm looking at the letter. We see that there's a letter between a Catholic and an Orthodox. A number of letters were exchanged. The letter we have here is dated the 6th of July, 1992; but if you look at the content of the letter itself, you see that reference is made to a first answer dated 10th of June. That was an answer to a letter sent initially on the 10th of March, 10th of March, 1992; in other words, before the events of May 1992. This Catholic priest is writing to his Orthodox counterpart to talk about something. We don't know what. His Orthodox counterpart responds on the 10th of June. And on the 6th of July, the Catholic priest writes another letter; and in that letter - and you're right, it may be the link - at paragraph 4, he draws the attention of his Orthodox counterpart on the situation in Hrtkovci. But when looking at this letter, there's something that we do not understand. We do not know why did he write to him in March. We have no idea why he wrote to him in March, what about. But you're right, the link can be established thanks to the fourth paragraph, because this Catholic priest, in July, a few weeks after May, draws the attention of his counterpart on what happened in Hrtkovci. But what you're saying about the seminar in 2002 is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, first, a comment regarding the letter. Obviously, it seems from the letter itself, the first paragraph, that there has been -- there had been an exchange of letters between these two priests, and this letter was not specially made to send it just because of a particular issue, but obviously was one of a series of letters. I, of course, agree with that. But, well, in the fourth paragraph, as you have just mentioned, is the link to the list, so it wouldn't -- it's rather straightforward to associate the list with the letter. As I'm saying, there are a few pages in the book just before the letter which are not attached here, in which a seminar of the priests from this area is summarised. But even without this seminar and the discussion that took place at the seminar, and obviously were partly related to the population situation in the region, I believe the bishop really needed to have good reasons to send this kind of letter to the patriarch, Pavle. Otherwise, I think, why would he do that? It's a high-level correspondence, in my view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, beyond the possible link between this letter and the list, one question: If I understand correctly, you cannot confirm that this letter was joined to the list. You can't confirm that this letter was attached to the list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is a correct observation. I cannot confirm that the two things were sent together. That is -- that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that it is absolutely impermissible for the alleged demographic expert of the OTP to say here, I quote, "I believe that the bishop had good reasons to write to the patriarch." It's not for her to think or believe. She has to say what statistical method she uses to link this letter with the list. Where is her scientific elaboration there? It's not for her to think that the bishop had good reasons. Is she here or was she brought here to think, to think in the courtroom? This is the most ridiculous thing that we've heard so far in relation to these alleged expert witnesses of the OTP. She thinks, she says that she thinks. Unbelievable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, two comments. On several occasions, you used the word "the alleged expert." You know full well that Ms. Tabeau has been acknowledged as an expert witness by a great number of Trial Chambers at this Tribunal. A number of people have acknowledged that she is competent in terms of demography, so no need to use that sort of language, "alleged expert." That's the first thing. The second thing about this letter: From what I understood, and you probably understood the same thing, this letter is to be found in the book written by a priest about several events, including about what happened to the Croats in Hrtkovci. This letter is to be found in the book. In the book, you also find the list. The OTP, probably in connection with Ms. Tabeau, the OTP decided that this letter may be relevant, because at the first paragraph of the letter, you find that in July 1992, the bishop who is in Djakovo, the bishop therefore is telling his Orthodox counterpart that there is a problem. That's to be found at paragraph 4 of the letter. Now, the question is: What is this problem? Well, the problem is probably related to the departure of Croats from Hrtkovci. That's it. Now, if you look at the letter, at the list, the book, and the events, you can see that a link has been established. Well, it may very well be that the bishop was mistaken in his analysis of the situation, and Ms. Tabeau stated earlier on that the bishop may have had very good reasons to write this. But we don't know and you don't know where the bishop had found information about these events, how he was informed about this. We have no idea about that. You may decide to call this bishop as a witness if that appears necessary. But as things stand, what we have is a letter dated July 1992 between two high-level officials of the church, and they mentioned something that happened in Hrtkovci. It may very well be that the patriarch responded to that letter. He certainly probably responded to that letter, but we don't have that response. It may be interesting to find out what is said in response, and you may wish to ask him the copy of that letter. Well, we'll proceed; but before that, we'll give an MFI number. One moment. I'll give you the floor later on, but first we need to have an MFI number, and the Trial Chamber will rule after your cross-examination. What did you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I want to tell you that I'm not going to call Ms. Tabeau an alleged expert any longer. I will try to imagine that she's a real expert. Now, what does this letter, nevertheless, have to do with her expertise? That's the core of the matter. This letter could have accompanied the testimony of an ordinary witness. Marko Kljajic, the author of the book, could have been brought in by the OTP. That would have been a real treat. For reasons unknown, the OTP didn't want to call Marko Kljajic as a witness, but they keep offering his book. All right. They can offer his book along with ordinary witnesses, but not along with a demographical statistical expert, because this letter has absolutely nothing to do with demography or statistics; only if she had made statistics for us to the effect of how many letters does the bishop send every year and/or the correspondence between the Orthodox patriarch and the Catholic bishop. Then that could be linked up to statistics. Now, just this letter, having just one single letter planted along with the expertise, the expert report of a demographical and statistical nature, that is absolutely impossible. This expert has nothing whatsoever to do with this letter, or can this expert explain this letter, or can this expert present what it is that she thinks about this letter. What do we care what she thinks about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, your comments are on the transcript now, but we need to give a number to this document, an MFI number. And as I said before giving you the floor, the Trial Chamber will rule on this document after your cross-examination and after re-examination. Mr. Registrar, we need a number for this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 2154A will be MFI P569.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. For the transcript, I want to add that Exhibit 2154A is made up of two documents; first, a letter from the Bishop Kos, dated 6th of July, 1992, that is the first document. Then we have a second document. It's a list of Croats from that settlement, a list that is also to be found in the book written by the Catholic priest. This number relates to two documents. The Trial Chamber will eventually rule on the letter. Please proceed, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, if I can now direct your attention to the next tab, which should be 65 ter number 4225. Is that exhibit also a source that you consulted for the compilation of your report for this case?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you, very briefly, describe what that is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is yet another list that was used to compile the integrated list presented in annex A of my report. This list was obtained in response to the RFA, request for assistance, sent by the OTP to the Croatian government in 2005. This list was submitted together with the list of refugees we just discussed, and some other things. So this list contains information about 200 individuals. These individuals largely were listed in the book of Marko Kljajic among the 280 families. Specifically, 97 family heads listed in the book of Marko Kljajic are also included in this list that was submitted to us completely separately by the Croatian authorities in response to our RFA. The list in the book of Marko Kljajic is incomplete. It only includes family heads. This is why we have 280 records on this list. However, in the book, it says that 805 persons are represented by the 280 families. So, naturally, we wanted a complete record of information about all 805 persons. Croatian authorities, within a relatively short period of time, were able to provide us with this list of 202 persons, among which 97 are the heads reported among the 280. So it is just an expansion of the list from the book of Marko Kljajic. Unfortunately, again, it is an incomplete expansion. Due to the short deadlines we had at that time, we obtained only the list of 202, and no more than that. Again, a very unfortunate thing, but it's better to have records of 202 persons than only the list of the -- from the book of Marko Kljajic. The record of information is far more complete than what we see in the book of Marko Kljajic. We have much more than just the first name and family name. We have here father's name, date of birth; we have address; we have the date of departure; we have the new address in Croatia; et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please try to shed some light on the following mystery. Please have a look at the list, at number 1 on this list, Ivan Akrap. We know that he was born on the 28th of April, 1960. We also can see that his father's name was Ante. We know his address -- not in Hrtkovci. No, we don't know it. It's unknown. The mystery for me lies at the next line. What do I find here? I find the following: "First registered in Croatia, 2nd of February, 1982, Zagreb." Then we have the address, number 16 Jure Kastelana Street. Apparently Mr. Akrap lived in Croatia in 1982. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible. Many people in the former Yugoslavia had their permanent place of residence in one of the former republics and worked in another. So for Croats from Vojvodina, it would be that some of them would have their jobs in Croatia, and they would travel systematically between these two places of residence. The same was the case in the population in Bosnia. So for those who travelled for jobs or just were there in Croatia for temporary jobs, it was, of course, obviously far easier in difficult times to go back to apply to be accepted in Croatia due to the situation in their permanent place of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This raises another legal matter. Looking at the case of Ivan Akrap, we can think that he was a legal resident of Croatia. We find the address that was his, and we see that he was registered. He has a name -- a registration number, 6251. At number 1, we have a Croat, a citizen of the Republic of Croatia, who was in Hrtkovci for some unknown reason, maybe to work there, but this person is a Croat and he's a Croat citizen. He has Croatian citizenship, and he goes home in 1992, apparently after the events. Is that the proper way to analyse this particular case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wouldn't interpret it this way. I would see Ivan Akrap as a person from Hrtkovci with his permanent place of residence in Hrtkovci. If you, Your Honours, compare this record with the record number 1 from the just-discussed list of 280 families, then you see that entry number 1 is Ivan Akrap from Hrtkovci, Ulica Lenjinova. The family size listed here is three persons. So the two lists are consistent. So the same person is reported in two sources: On the one hand, in the list of expelled persons from Hrtkovci, as the family head, number 1 on the list; and, at the same time, from the second list provided to us by the Croat authorities, we know this person obviously travelled between Croatia and Hrtkovci for whatever reason, most obviously I would think of a job in Croatia. And in 1992, the person and the family decided to leave Hrtkovci, as they are reported as persons who out-migrated from the village in the list of Marko Kljajic. That is my interpretation of these records.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that this document doesn't have any official designations. We can believe that the -- believe the expert that someone from the Croatian authorities gave this to her. Furthermore, the expert is allowing herself to speculate here. I do have to apologise for using the term "expert." If I were to use the feminine form in the Serbian, then it would mean "witch," literally, so that wouldn't be right. That's why I'm using the masculine.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is totally unacceptable, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you have just used unacceptable terms to call the expert we have in front of us. But you're telling us, madam, that the Croatian authorities sent you this document. That is a more comprehensive document than the others. But which authorities are we talking about? Are we talking about this office, about the labour ministry, about the interior ministry? Who sent you these documents, and how did they compile this document? There's a great deal of information here, to start with the fact that these people had been registered in the Republic of Croatia. There must be files somewhere. So who sent you this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The exact name of this organisation is the Office for Detained Persons -- Detained and Missing Persons in Zagreb. The head of this office is Colonel Grujic, and this list was compiled by his office. I believe - exactly, don't know - I believe this list was compiled based on their own searches in the official population register of Croatia, using the names of family heads from the first list. This is how was it made, in my view. So whoever was registered in the official records of Croat authorities is shown here in this list with all kinds of detailed about them. I want to stress that, in our request, we explicitly asked for records of expelled persons from Hrtkovci, who left Hrtkovci in 1992, and this was part of this response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So we now know that in Zagreb, you have an Office for Detained Persons and Missing Persons, with Mr. Grujic as its head, and that he's the one who sent you this list. It may have been a good idea to also provide the various correspondence related to that, but now at least we know where this document comes from. It was not clear at first sight. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to draw your attention, Mr. President, to the fact that Colonel Grujic was mentioned, but it's actually Ivan Grujic who figured here for over five years as an expert witness of the OTP for some other matters; and, recently, they withdrew him, assessing that his credibility had been challenged in some other trials. Now they replaced him with Anna Maria Bilic and this other expert. I can't remember exactly. I cannot tell you just off the cuff now. So, see, one suspicious circumstance accompanies another one. As soon as you're allowed to use a document that is not an official one or not designated as an official one, then there's a series of problems. Now, Ivan Grujic, even I've been taken by surprise. Although I have excellent intelligence services, I haven't come across this information. Now I'm really surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, Colonel Grujic, is he the Ivan Grujic who was supposed to testify as an expert witness and was then withdrawn from the list? Is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have to consult with wiser minds in my office to see if, indeed, it is the same. I believe it is not; but before I go on the record formally stating that, I'd like to check first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time, we would move for the admission of 65 ter number 4225.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll give an MFI number to that document as well. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI P570.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I would now like to turn your attention to what's in your binder as 65 ter number 2859E, so it's those sections that would come immediately after your report in the first binder. What I'd like to have you explain to the Trial Chamber is figure 7, which is listed as "Requests for certificates of christening by year of request." Again, that should be in your binder as 2859E.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Oh, I'm lost a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you have binder 1, or are you looking at binder 2?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: At binder 1. We're looking at binder 1 now; yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is just an extra presentation after the list we just discussed?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Can you find your report in the binder?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes. It's first, yeah. Oh, yes, yes, yes. I do have it. It's 02895E, right, you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct. And, actually, that is a page from your report at page 21; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: This is just an extract for simplicity. Could you, looking at figure 7, briefly describe to the Trial Chamber what that figure depicts?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: This is the timing of requests for certificates of christening shown here by year of request. The period covered by this figure is from 1949 until 2001. The births shown in the figure represents the overall number of requests for certificates of christening made in a given year. The first observation from this figure is that there is one very high peak on the figure for the year 1992. This bar, the highest bar, represents the 180 requests made in just this single year. So an extremely high number compared with all other years, compared to the year 1992, where 180 requests were made. In all other years, insignificant numbers are shown. There are also two different colours used in this figure: One is red, one is blue. These colours show a distinction between the requests made for individuals who died - that would be the red colour - and individuals for whom requests were made at the time that they were alive. It's normally the case that if a person dies, then a request is made in order to arrange a Catholic burial. So, normally, requests for surviving people wouldn't be made if there were no other reasons. For the red bars, we see that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, a request for what exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For the certificate of christening. Certificate of christening is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. Would there be a request for christening for someone who had died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If a Catholic burial is going to be arranged in another place by another Catholic priest than the one from Hrtkovci, then they would need a certificate for christening of this person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, this chart on figure 7 is striking, especially so since it's in colour, which is really good. What I note, but I'm sure that everyone in this courtroom can note the same thing, what I note is this: We see that from 1949 to 1971, there were requests for christening certificates, but only for people who had passed away. At the time, no certificates of christening were asked, requested for living people. And a witness explained to us, saying out of memory, that under the communist regime, it was not very good to say that you were a Catholic, which is why probably certificates of christening were not requested. However, and now this is where I run into a problem, it's true that in 1992 there are 180 requests. Obviously, something happened. But why is it that in 1989, 1990, and 1991, there were some requests for these certificates of christening? How can you explain that? 1992, okay, we know that events took place, and one could understand what happened. But why is it that before, the three years before, there were some requests? It's on your chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are. It is not that I can explain by giving you concrete reasons why, because I didn't study the reasons why these requests were made. If it would be my personal opinion, unsupported with any material, I would think of a changing political situation in the former Yugoslavia. I would think of 1989, about Kosovo and the speech by Slobodan Milosevic on Kosovo Polje; and generally the situation becoming politically more and more unstable and, well, more and more ethnic clashes were happening at this time. But this is not my expert opinion; and, as I said, I didn't study any underlying causes for the requests presented in this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm talking to the expert here. When you look at the figures, and you see the figures of the people who are leaving the settlement as of 1989, does this mean that as of 1989 there's already an out-flow of people starting? These people are going to Croatia, aren't they? A number of witnesses came here and told us and explained that in order to go to Croatia, in order to cross the border in the first place, one had to prove Croatian ethnicity or Catholicism, and having a certificate of christening could prove you were Catholic. So could you tell us that as of 1989, there was a migratory outflow which may have to do with Milosevic's speech in 1989? I don't know, but you're the expert here; and in your report, you want to demonstrate that in 1992 a number of Croats left. So I would like to know whether Croats didn't leave beforehand, because it seems to be what you have on your chart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's right, some left before 1992, and this is what is shown on the chart. Well, we shouldn't forget that population movement always in there, in any area. It is any country that people go out and come in; and, obviously, there were some migratory movements already before 1992. Only the difference is, for 1992, we know exactly that those who left the village took the direction of Croatia. So that's the difference. If we could study the destination of those who left before, we -- I am thinking of people who left this area and moved to other countries, for instance, the out-migration from the region of the former Yugoslavia was enormous, and it was -- it did not start exactly with the beginning of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And chart number 8 helps us go into details regarding this issue. In 1992, you state that 180 people leave; and on figure 8, we have more details regarding this. We note that before May, even before May 6th, people were already leaving. In January 1992, maybe one or two people made a request. In February, there's twice the number. March, it's doubled again. In April, before the speech was actually made and delivered, obviously there are at least five or six people who are asking for this christening certificate. Then we have a peak in May and June, and then it tapers down. So, as an expert, can you say that even before May 1992, there were requests for christening certificates involving about a few dozens of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is what I'm saying. So I am not saying that the out-migration started rapidly in May and continued only in May and June until August. So the region was affected by some factors that caused people to move out in the entire year of 1992; although obviously most intensively, unquestionably intensively, it was May and June, as shown on this chart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's quite striking in your chart. In May and June, there's about 70 people every month that are asking for these christening certificates. Ms. Biersay, the Registrar is telling me that you have ten minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
