utterances.text: In that vein, if you could, in the same -- under the same tab, turn to page 23, the extracted page 23. Your Honour has covered figure 8 with you, which is on page 21. I'd now like to direct your attention to figure 9 on page 23. Looking at that figure, were you able to identify a peak month or peak months for the requests that were made for christening certificates?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Actually, figure 9 is showing the distribution by day of request. In two months, in May and June, the left chart shows the date for May and the right one for June. So, here, the bars represent the daily number of requests. So it's striking, then, in May, the first requests were made on the 8th of May and then continued intensively until the end of May. The highest number is seen for the 15th of May and the days thereafter, 16th, 19th. And on the right chart, we see also in the first half of June, the number of requests, daily number of requests, was high. So it is even not the two whole months, but May, starting the 8th of May until the end, and the first half of June, where the numbers are extraordinary high.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You discuss in your report also your reliance on the requests made for marriage records from the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you do a similar comparison as far as the timing of the request for marriage records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And how did the timing compare to the ones that we've just discussed for christening records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is very similar; very, very similar, really. Most -- the most requests for marriage certificates were made again in 1992; actually, 82 of 94 requests, as far as I remember. So 82 out of 94 or something like that were made in 1992; and the remaining requests were made, a few of them, in the later years, but in the 1990s. That is one observation. And within the year of 1992, it was the month of June where the highest number of requests were made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Witness, before talking about these marriage certificates, let's take a look at the technique used, and go back to table 9, please. We see that on May 8, there are three requests for a christening certificate; then, on May 10, we have two requests; on May 12th, two; May 13th, four; May 14th, two. Then there's a peak which you told us about on May 15, because on May 15 there are ten requests. Then, when I go back to figure 7, where I see the figures from March, April, January, February, I see that there are requests. I don't see any speeding up in this process there. So maybe the speech made on May 6th had a certain influence, but if there has been an influence, maybe there's a time lag before the effect is actually felt in time. Here, it seems that it took about 15 days for the effect to be felt -- no, ten days, between May 6th and May 15. But after May 15, we see that there's still an even number of requests up until June 10th. So, this being said, I wondered the following, and I wonder whether you investigated this. This is what I wondered. We have the figures, of course, but we have to explain these figures; otherwise, you know, just figures by themselves are not sufficient. We need to understand the figures. We were told that the people who crossed the border had to produce documents, certificates, possibly christening certificates. So the people who obtained these christening certificates, I would like to know whether they immediately left or whether they took some time before leaving. Let's take the example of a person who's requesting a christening certificate on May 10th. When's he going to leave Hrtkovci; on May 15, in June? I'm sure you can't tell us, so I don't think you really went into such detail. So we don't really know whether these people who obtained their christening certificate leave immediately once they have the paper in hand, but let's assume that they leave very fast, that they leave almost immediately. I would like to know whether you checked whether they were leaving in convoys, in organised convoys, or whether they were just leaving on their own, by themselves. I assume that, you know, they had to pick up their belongings, their pets, so they needed either to have a private car or there needed to be a bus or trucks. So were there organised departures, or is it the fact that at the OTP no one really investigated this? Because if Croatia regulated the influx of refugees, which could be understood, of course, this might explain why these requests for christening certificates seem to be scheduled over time in an organised fashion. Did you envisage all these assumptions; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't investigate the ways of departing, and I'm calling the requests for certificates a proxy for departures. This is how the information should be understood. This is a proxy. That means an approximation. It is an explicit expression of the intention to depart. I don't know whether there were buses, whether there were organised convoys, anything of this. I don't know that. There must be, of course, a lag, I guess, time lag between the decision and the departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, can I just put another question in follow-up of what the Presiding Judge has just asked you. If you look at the table number 9, you see that there is a peak apparently on the 15th, 16th, and 19th of May in requests for christening certificates, and then it appears that there's another peak in June, on June 10th. Did you make any attempt to explain why these peaks occurred on these days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, if I may add, I believe not all requests for certificates were registered in the parish books. I believe there were more requests made, and not all of them are on paper. As far as I know, some people were afraid of being registered as having requested their certificates. For whatever reason, they didn't want to leave this on paper. And if you compare the number of requests for both marriage and christening certificates with the number of individuals represented by the list from the Marko Kljajic book, then of course the number from the book is much higher. If all those people reported on this list, which would be 805, have requested the certificates, then the numbers would be much higher, of course. But whether or not this would have impact on the peaks, I believe not really, because these requests from the parish books are a representative sample, I believe, of all the requests. So the timing can be seen as a representation of the overall timing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you investigate the use of these christening certificates? I'm sure that you had some working meetings with trial attorneys at the OTP, but I'd like to know whether you investigated, whether you checked whether it's the Croatian authorities that had asked for these marriage certificates, who would have told people, "We don't mind welcoming Catholic Serbian nationals who may be of Croatian ethnicity as long as they have a christening certificate," as that might explain why there are so many christening certificates and so many requests for this. Did you look into this while you were compiling your report? Your report shows that something happening, obviously. Suddenly, we have all these requests for christening certificates that crop up, but, I mean, there must be an explanation. So do you believe that it is the persons themselves who, on their own volition, decided that they needed to have their christening certificate, if need be; or was it because the Croatian authorities had very specifically asked for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we -- I don't think Croatian authorities denied that this was required from the people from this area to be accepted; but at the same time, they didn't provide the copies of the certificates to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But what would if I told you that a witness told us that exactly, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What can I say to this? I don't have any certificates from the Croatian authorities. This is my answer.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's move to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If I could now direct your attention to, again, your binder, just the next tab, which is 65 ter number 2859F, which is also page 10 of your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Biersay, I forgot to ask you whether you wanted a number for the tables we've just examined, 7, 8 and 9; or, for you, are they part and parcel of the report of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do believe that they are part and parcel of the report. The only question that I would pose to the Chamber is, if the Chamber would find the colour useful in its deliberation, then I could move for the admission of this or resubmit a colour version that might be helpful with the graphs and the like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll ask my fellow Judges, but it's true that when you have coloured graphs, coloured charts, it's easier. Yes, of course. We'll give a number, then, to the previous document. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter number 2589E will be P571. It will be admitted and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In the preparation of your report, did you consult any census data?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, we did. The two censuses, 1991 and 2002, aggregate statistics obtained from statistical authority in Serbia were used.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the census for 1991, approximately how many people were reported as living in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: These numbers are all reported in table 1, so it is perhaps easier if you look at the table 1 to see the numbers. So the Hrtkovci was a small village, as a matter of fact. Approximately, 2.500 people lived there at the time of the 1991 census. Of those, about 1.000 Croats and 500 Serbs, 500 Hungarians, 400 Yugoslavs, and the rest were remaining were ethnicities. So the ethnic composition in Hrtkovci was actually with a majority of Croats. That wouldn't be an absolute term, "majority," it would be a relative, "majority." That would be about 40 per cent of the Hrtkovci population in 1991. The Serbs were represented at 21 per cent, Hungarians 19 per cent, Yugoslavs about 17 per cent. So it was obviously a multi- ethnic village with all ethnicities' major groups, I mean, living in Vojvodina represented in the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: In comparing the 1991 census with the 2002 census, were you able to discern any increases or decreases in the number of non-Serbs in that village?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the non-Serb population, especially of Croats, Hungarians, and Yugoslavs, declined very considerably between the two censuses, the 1991 and 2002 census. This is shown in table 1 and also in figure 2 that represents the data from table 1. So for these groups that I just mentioned, the Croats, Hungarians, and Yugoslavs, considerable declines occurred between these two censuses. Altogether, these three groups declined by 1.283 persons, which is by a drop of 76 per cent, approximately; and the other groups, most importantly the Serbs, increased. The number of them increased between these two censuses from 500, approximately, to 2.400 in 2002, which is a very high increase of 357 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Tabeau, can we just, for clarification, ask you to clarify whether a Yugoslav is defined as being a non-Serb, or is a Yugoslav defined as someone who has not given any information about his or her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yugoslavs, sir, are people who reported themselves as Yugoslavs to the question about their ethnic affiliation in both censuses. In both censuses, this question was an open-ended question. That means everybody could report whatever the person wanted to. So Yugoslavs are most definitely not those who didn't report any ethnicity or had unknown ethnicity. They just reported themselves as Yugoslavs. In most cases, it would be people from mixed marriages, for instance. So this group is separated here because it is just a separate ethnic group at the time of 1991 and the time of 2002. Both are present in the data, in this data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm asking because in your report you refer to other non-Serbs as being, for instance, Hungarians or Yugoslavs, and this may lead one to think that a Yugoslav is defined as being a non-Serb.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Actually, I would think of them as non-Serbs because they had the opportunity to declare themselves as Serbs in the census and they didn't. They choose the option Yugoslavs, which is an expression of being not a Serb, a Croat, a Hungarian, a German, anybody else, just a Yugoslav. This issue comes in several discussions back and back again, and I believe, myself, and strongly so, that this was a separate group of people, an ethnic group, Yugoslavs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if we look at the bar charts with the 2002 census in red and the 1991 census in black, it's a very clear chart. We can all have a look at the chart and then look at the table, where we have detailed figures about the number of inhabitants and their distribution according to their sex and ethnicity. In this chart, we can see without any doubt that the Serbs constitute the majority in 2002. In 2002, the Serbs in the village account for 2.396 inhabitants. In 1991, there were 531 of them. But did you know that these Serbs, the Serbs in the village, had been expelled from Krajina, themselves? Were you aware of this? You must have been told about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, most likely there are in-comers among the population of the 2002, and most likely they are from -- these are Croatian Serbs who entered in this village as well, as they did in other places in Vojvodina, of course. It is impossible that a normal demographic growth of the population would result from 500 in 2000 and 400 within ten years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wouldn't it have been possible to study the arrival of these expelled Serbs and look at what time they arrived in great numbers? Because I suppose that when they arrived, they must have been registered in Hrtkovci, but it's something you didn't look into, or maybe you did. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is most certainly them registered in Serbia. The authorities also had registration of internally displaced persons and refugees; and at that time, already the registration existed and all persons, in-comers from Croatia, were in the system. I don't have the data on this, but it is correct that data exists that would allow to study the arrivals of the Croatian Serbs in Vojvodina and other areas of Serbia. I requested this data already, I think, in 2003, but never received, under the excuse that the data is confidential and cannot be shared, which is not true because I have the same data for Bosnia and Herzegovina, for instance. Well, not having the data, of course, doesn't mean that no analysis is possible, not having, I mean, individual data on arrivals; but I had some aggregate statistics which I included in my report. There is a table in the report, and this is table 6, page 18 in the report. This table comes from the Yugoslav survey, which is an official journal published by Serb authorities. There are scientific articles on all kinds of issues. Among others, this one article was about the data from the registration of internally displaced persons and refugees in Serbia, in Serbia and Montenegro, I should say, at that time. The data comes from a very large survey conducted in 1996. That would be a perfect moment after the war in Bosnia ended and huge waves of Croatian Serbs arrived in the Serbian territory after Operation Storm and Flash. Here, in this table, data is shown by the time of arrival; and not only that; this is one aspect of arrival in Serbia. The other aspect shown here is the country of origin. One of the countries of origin of the arrivals of refugees and other war-affected persons, as they are called, is Croatia, Croatia. As we see, we have two figures for Croatia by the end of 1991 and in 1992. So the refugees from Croatia registered in Serbia; refugees and war-affected persons, I should say - that is an important distinction. By the end of 1991, there were 56.194 individuals registered as arrivals from Croatia, all territories, not only the Republika Srpska Krajina but also remaining territories of Croatia; and in 1992, there are 34.119 arrivals. So, altogether, these two numbers give a total of approximately 90.000 arrivals. That is based on data coming from a very good source, very reliable, and we can further conclude that that is the number that could be maximally expected in Vojvodina. But not all arrivals ended in Vojvodina. There is another table in this report, table 5 on the previous page, where I show how many of the arrivals were in Vojvodina and how many in Serbia. So about 40 per cent of the arrivals were in Vojvodina. I'm speaking of the total of the arrivals. That would be a much larger total because it would relate to the entire conflict period, 1991 until 1996 even.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. If you allow me, I'd like to follow up on the question put to you by my fellow Judge. I have the following question with respect to statistics: In 1991, 426 people declared themselves as Yugoslavs. In 2002, 67 declared themselves as Yugoslavs. So over the space of ten years, if we compare these two figures, about 360 individuals changed their ethnicity. What about these 360 individuals? Well, they can be either Croats, Serbs, or Hungarians. These 360 individuals are to be distributed amongst these three categories. If we assume that all of these 360 individuals were Croats, it's impossible, statistically speaking, it's impossible, I know, it's impossible. But the Croats who were 504 in 1991, there would have been more of them if you take these -- at least a third of these 360 people into account. But in 2002, we find that the number of Croats drops to 256, and the Croatian population is valued by two, roughly. Are you following what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So every second Croat left the village by 2002, but there's something that I find rather surprising. Out of these 256 Croats, we have 110 men and 146 women. But if you look at all the other figures, you have roughly the same number of men and women. If you look above, you have 504 men and 502 women. That's obvious because at birth you have about one boy for every girl born. Where does this deficit come from in 2002, this deficit of 30 men? Could you provide a statistical or demographical explanation for us, because we should have the same number of men and women. But here we find there are 30 men less; whereas, if you look at the Serbs, you have the same number of men and women, 1.197 men and 1.197 women. Could you provide an explanation for this or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have some comments. First of all, this -- the population is shown in this table on two different moments of time: Ethnicity in the 1991 census and later in the 2002 census. The definition of ethnicity in each census is based on the data collected in this census. There is no guarantee that persons who reported themselves as Croats remained Croats in the next census. And this is right that particularly among Yugoslav people tendered to change their report on ethnicity depending on the situation, political basic situation at the time the census was conducted. It's possible that some Yugoslavs indeed declared themselves as Serbs in the 2002 census. So this presentation is in some way biased because of the changing perceptions of ethnicity among the respondents of the census. That is one remark. So, ideally, the change in the ethnic composition should be assessed by using a different approach, which we tried to do in this project; but in order to do this, I would need individual census records from both censuses. By linking these records at the individual level, I could compare the ethnic group -- groups as reported in one of the censuses. In this case, I would choose, of course, the 1991 census as the basis for this comparison. I could not do that because the data was not provided to me by the Serb statistical authorities, again being confidential. But as we know, regulations can be done in order to prevent the confidentiality and the data could have been provided. So that is one thing. So I can't explain these kind of changes by directly linking the census 1991 with the census 2002. As it comes to the sex distribution, of course we can look at the sex distribution as reported in these two years, and we can try to assess this distribution. It is, indeed, the right observation that for some groups, as for Serbs, for instance, the distribution is more or less 50/50. But the change -- the sex distribution is dependent on the age structure of the population. The older the population, the less men are reported; and, for sure, the age structure among the ethnic groups in the former Yugoslav was not the same. The Croat population was known to have an older age structure, so that might be one explanation for the less men. But another explanation is that, who knows, perhaps more men left the village. We still see the number of the, say, missing Croats in 2002 is 750 as compared with the 1991 census. So this population did not recover by 2002 and is much, much smaller than what was reported in 1991. The opposite is for the Serbs. Well, for Hungarians, there is a decline, considerable decline, as we see; and for Yugoslavs, there is a decline, but part of this decline might be related to the change of ethnicity reported in the 2002 census.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will need to have our last break. We'll resume after a break. I believe that the Prosecutor has two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I have one question left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please put your question to the witness, then.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you compare for the Trial Chamber the decrease in the Croat population, when you look at the two censuses that you discuss, with annex A that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the annex A contains records of 722, say about 700 persons; and the decline which we still observe by 2002 is 750 persons. So I wouldn't call it a coincidence, just only, you know, because I made this list. There is an unquestionable observation that the population of Croats declined between the two censuses and that most obviously people were living in the village. The question is when they were living in the village. From the analysis of timing, it is clear it was - I did it for the entire period, even for 2002 - it is clear the maximum numbers were seen for 1992. Why they were leaving is a question I couldn't answer in this report, for all kinds of reasons. First of all, I didn't look at the causes explicitly, but by using sources that I would collect for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And at this time, Your Honour, the Prosecution would move for the admission of 65 ter number 2859F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 2859F will be MFI P572. And just to clarify, the previous document, which was 65 ter number 2585E will be MFI P571.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. We'll now break for 20 minutes. We'll resume around a quarter past 12.00, and Mr. Seselj will be able to start his cross-examination. That will obviously continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I owed the Trial Chamber some information with respect to Ivan Grujic, and I can now confirm for the Court that it is the same person. So the person who is replaced on the witness list is also the person with whom the RFA information was coordinated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew that before, Judges, and I was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, you were born in Poland, were you not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I have dual nationality, Polish and Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I didn't mean "nationality." Perhaps the interpretation was wrong. I meant "ethnicity." In Serbian, when you say "nacionalnost," it implies "ethnicity." So what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My answer would still be the same, Polish and Dutch.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, were your mother and father Dutch?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: No. My mother and father were both Polish. Your Honour, if I may make a remark. If there are going to be private questions to me, I feel I have the right to protect my privacy, and I don't want to discuss these private issues in an open session. I feel this is my private life, and I want to protect it for business here. That is as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if you want to deal with private matters regarding our witness, let me tell you that the witness is asking for private session to discuss these issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am absolutely not interested in the private life of this witness, and I don't know why the witness is suddenly so afraid. I have nothing further to ask her. What I'm interested in is the ethnicity of the witness and her religious affiliation, and that must be done in public session. That's all I'm interested in, her religion and her ethnicity, and she has to give me an answer publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe there was an interpretation problem. It's your religious faith that Mr. Seselj is interested in. Do you believe that this is part of your private life or can you want to an in open session, or do you want a private session for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me already about my parents and what nationality were they, and I believe my religion, my values and morals, are my private life, so I insist to answer these kind of questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber has deliberated on this issue and believes that regarding religious faith, if the witness doesn't want to answer, she doesn't have to answer. It's her own free will, which is normal. She said that she would not answer it, and she won't answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will withdraw that question because I consider that there is a reason for which the witness is ashamed to say what her ethnicity is and what her religion is, but I'm no longer interested in that. All I'm doing is observing that the witness did not want to answer the question and that she must have a strong reason for that, which means she's ashamed of her ethnicity and religion. Let me draw your attention to one more thing. This is not the first case of this kind. There were other experts like that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, the witness is not ashamed or anything. She told you that her parents were Polish. Very well. And regarding her religion faith, she just won't say anything. That's the end of the question. Move to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, what happened was that I asked about her ethnicity, that is, her ethnic affiliation, and the witness kept insisting upon her citizenship. I'd just like to remind you that we had a similar case with Anthony Oberschall and with Mr. Riedlmayer, the same case exactly, that they were avoiding stating their ethnicity. I can draw my own conclusions about that, but I'm not going to deal with that anymore, and I'm going to move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: For eight years, you've been working in the Tribunal's OTP; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did it come about that you gained employment with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I applied for a job and was accepted out of about 60 candidates who applied as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was it a public job announcement?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was announced on the web site of the United Nations and this Tribunal, so it was a public announcement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what were the requirements of the job?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, there is a job description that was placed on the internet at that time, and the requirements are specified there. So there was a whole list, long list of requirements; and, obviously, I fulfilled this entire list.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: With respect to the requirements, I'm just interested in one thing, and that is whether that job announcement put up -- whether The Hague Tribunal was asking for an expert of the demographic branch. Did they ask for a demographer or was it a general announcement and competition for different various professions?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It was an announcement for a demographer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And of 60 demographers, they chose you. Is that how I'm to understand your answer?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about the other 59 persons who applied, whether or not they were all demographers or just social scientists, but obviously I was chosen as the best applicant among all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But if the job announcement asked for a demographer, it is understood that all the candidates, all the applicants, must be demographers if they meet the requirements of the job description?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I believe so. This is the title I have, and this is the title I have been using officially in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: How can I know about other candidates? I wasn't on the panel who were interviewing the candidates. I was just one of the candidates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I assume you followed the outcome of the announcement. You had people you knew in the OTP who gave you that information, how the process was progressing.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, not -- I didn't know the people at the OTP. Actually, this is my husband who had found at that time the announcement on the UN web site and told me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mmm-hmm. Now, how would you explain the concept of a refugee? How would you define "refugee"?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the definition one uses. There is a legal definition that is used by authorities in the countries in the former Yugoslavia and other countries who collect information and register internally-displaced persons and refugees, and there is also a statistical definition that I used myself in several studies I presented at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Give us that definition, at long last.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Which one do you want, legal or statistical?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The one you know.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the legal definition would include the fact that a person, a refugee, is somebody who left their own place of residence and their own country, and they didn't leave voluntarily but they left because of being persecuted or because of the fear of being persecuted, due to reasons as racial, ethnic, whatever other reasons. What matters is the fear of being actually persecuted. The statistical definition is different from legal, in the sense that what we did in the past in several projects. We compared the place of residence of individuals at the outbreak of the conflict and after the end of the conflict; and based on the comparison of the places, we drew conclusions about whether or not the person became displaced or a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Your colleagues in the OTP instructed you well. You gained a great deal of experience in other trials to waste as much time as possible during the cross-examination. You could have given us a much simpler answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection to that characterization. The running commentary on the witness's answers is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Refrain from making comments, please, and making running commentaries. You asked a question on the definition of refugees. Our witness -- the witness gave us the definition according to the Geneva Conventions in 1951 that we all know, then she gave the statistical definition of "refugees." She gave a good answer, so why do you add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Now let's simplify that. Now listen to me carefully. A refugee is, therefore, in the simplest possible terms, an individual who feels certain danger and is trying to escape from that danger, because in the word "refugee," there is this few -- there is this concept of a person running away, faced with a danger, whether real or imagined. That's not important, but he is fleeing his own country. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the danger of, you said, the fear is one thing, but in the same definition, that the person is actually persecuted; this is either/or. So you are right, generally speaking, either being persecuted or feeling this fear to be persecuted. I'm not instructed by the OTP, if I may comment on the other questions that you had to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, I am now using the less extreme word. "Persecution" is the more extreme. What I'm saying is that it's enough for the person or refugee to feel fear, to flee his country because of that fear, whether it is real or imagined. So that is the lowest level at which this term "refugee" can be applied. With "persecution," of course, we don't need to use many words to talk about that; right? So it's the fear of -- the fear of danger. I'm being very mild in saying that it need not even be realistic fear; it can be imagined fear, perceived fear. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I could not imagine that the fear is something imagined. You either have the feeling, the fear, or not. That is how it is. This is how I see it, simply speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I didn't say that fear was imaginary, but danger was imaginary. Fear is a subjective category, and danger is an objective category, for the most part. So don't try and reverse what I've said. Now, somebody who is fleeing is leaving something behind him, and that something is, first of all, property, immovables, but very often movable property, too, because they can't carry everything with them; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Can we then, according to you as a demographer, a professional who knows the legal definition and demographic definition of "refugee," can we call a refugee somebody who for certain reasons, whatever those reasons may be, has the time to find somebody with whom he will exchange his property and draw up a contract about that, register it with the court in question, and having drawn up a contract and made it official, organise his leaving? Can such a person be called a refugee at all?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, if the exchange is voluntary and from both sides voluntary, then it is voluntary and there is no fear, I guess. But it's all about whether or not exchanges were voluntary in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And for you to check and see whether the exchange was voluntary, you would have to look at the exchange agreements and contracts and to compare the property that was being exchanged; right? That was the only exact manner of verifying this; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I didn't study the exchanges. If I had a project on exchanging property, then most certainly I would collect -- would collect other sources than what I used in my report. I didn't study it. It is not the study of my report, exchanges of the property.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, that's why I'm asking you because it isn't the subject of your report; whereas, you allow yourself, in your report, to speak about refugees and displaced persons. Whereas, you don't have a single piece of evidence and proof to show that a single Croat from Hrtkovci or Vojvodina can be considered a refugee at all. You must have an objective, material piece of proof and evidence to show that the person was actually a refugee; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the official piece I have is the list of 116 refugees that I obtained from the Croatian authorities. This is the list of legal refugees in Croatia. And in this list, if you study it, for some persons remarks are made relating to their property, and some involuntary exchanges or just lost property are mentioned. But you are right that I don't have the actual contract of exchange, any kind of document that would be associated with these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Let's leave behind the Croatian authorities, state authorities, that they are a relevant source of information. Had they been a relevant source of information, they would have been called in here to testify by the Prosecutor and show on the basis of books that there are Croatian refugees from Vojvodina. You are the Prosecution expert witness here now, and now I'm asking you to show me any evidence whatsoever on the basis of which you are able to say with certainty that such-and-such a person, just one man, one person, a refugee, is a refugee, in the sense that fleeing from some danger because of his fear, he left behind his property and sought refuge in another state. You don't have any such proof or evidence, do you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Except for the list of 116, plus the analysis of the census records, 1991 versus 2002, in which it's clear some people had to leave their property behind. Except for other data on the departures from Hrtkovci, I don't have any other evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, you cannot make a single conclusion saying that people left their property behind. Nobody left their property behind. All the people who left exchanged their property. Maybe you can find someone somewhere that had sold his property earlier on and went to Austria, Hungary, or goodness knows where else, but you don't have a shred of evidence to show that there was a single Croat from Vojvodina who, according to the legal definition from international law or the demographic definition, can be called a refugee; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, we just discussed the sources I used in my report, and these are the sources I have at my disposal and studied. I don't have any sources --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, we will come to the sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will get to the sources.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- please be allowed to continue instead of Mr. Seselj cutting her off, that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You had started an answer on line 22, 23, 24, and 25; and Mr. Seselj interrupted you. So could you complete your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to say I don't have sources that would report on the exchanged property or property that was sold or property that wasn't sold. I don't have these records, simply speaking; and this is clear from my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we've seen a number of witnesses here. Of course, you can imagine that since the trial started, we have heard a good number of witnesses. Out of memory, let me tell you that some witnesses said that they exchanged their flats, and we did see some exchange contracts by which flats were exchanged. This is a fact that we took due note of. Then, secondly, other witnesses said that the exchange had been encouraged or triggered, we don't really know who started, by the Croats or the Serbs. We even have a witness who told us that according to him, some kind of secret agreement had been made between Tudjman and Milosevic to order these population transfers. So we were told of all these events. If we assume that what all these witnesses told us was true, do you believe that this would have changed anything to your report and to the conclusions you actually drew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I would make any changes, I don't think so. My report remains as it is, and I was just answering the question related to whether I have any additional evidence related to the property. I don't. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You gave an answer when you were asked about the definition of "refugees." I was listening to you, and I was wondering at the same time whether demographers, in the framework of their studies, don't have the same definition of "refugees" as the Geneva Convention. Why don't they have their own perception of refugees? I'm not a demographer. I don't know what are the bases for all this, but why is it that your definition does not match the definition of "refugees" that is recognised in international law? Why is it that you have another approach in demography?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think we have another approach in demography. We fully respect the legal definitions as proposed by the Geneva Conventions. This is not about the different definitions that we use; and, of course, there are sources in every country which report separately about the legal -- legally-defined refugees or asylum-seekers and we often use this data. But at the same time, we in demography have the studies of migration in which we not necessarily use only the data on refugees and asylum-seekers. We would then use other data sources. There are plenty that can be used. On the first place, there are surveys which cover certain groups of migrants arriving or departing; and, well, in these sources, possibly the legal definitions would be used when asked what the reasons, right, et cetera. But the statistical definition I mentioned was actually the definition I used in my expert reports in this Tribunal. In the absence of sources that would report on the legally-understood refugees, I had to work with a definition that would bring me the results that were needed for my reports, and this is why the statistical definition, which is often used in demography, by the way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you use the word "refugee" in your report, if I understand correctly, the meaning you ascribe to this word of "refugee" can be the meaning defined under the Geneva Convention, but it can also be another meaning. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in this report. It is, in this report, the Geneva Convention. There is one source called "Refugee table," these 116 records; and this is the legal definition. The other sources I don't call "refugees" because I don't know, simply speaking. These are persons who left the village. Of many of them, it is known that they are called "expelled individuals," but this is not expelled -- well, I wouldn't dare to use the legal term "refugee," because I don't know how many of them, as a matter of fact, were recognised in Croatia as refugees and how many were not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I get your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, as a scientist, if you establish that someone is a refugee, you look at the definition from the Geneva Conventions, from international law in general. That is what you use as your yardstick, not how the Croatian authorities registered a particular person. What do you care about how the Croatian authorities registered a certain person, or are you putting your full trust in the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: It is not me who is the authority entitled to make decisions about whether or not a person, a migrant arriving in a country, is a refugee. So it is that, in every country, there is an authority who is entitled, who has in its mandate to make these kind of legal decisions. I have to rely on the data provided by this authority, and this is what I did in this case. I can't dismiss every source based on reasons like, you know, whether a person is likable to me or not. There is an authority. There is an authority who has it in its mandate, and I have no reasons to disbelieve this authority, but I just use the data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: As a demographer, you could observe certain movements of the population, and there's no denying that. There were movements of the population. One of the elements of this movement is the movement of Croatian population from Serbia towards Croatia. But as a scientist and as a Prosecution expert, you had to have irrefutable proof that these were refugees, not just a piece of paper given to you by the Croatian authorities without any official designation and in which they say such-and-such persons are refugees. How could you accept that? So you've already taken sides, with one particular side in a civil war. What the Croatian authorities gave to you is irrefutable for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm having trouble finding the question in Mr. Seselj's monologue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not a question for Ms. Biersay. It's a question for the Prosecution expert. Ms. Biersay, I'm not putting a question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, you were asked a question, and I understood that question, but can you answer the question or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I can. I haven't taken sides with anybody. I must say I made a lot of efforts to be as objective as possible. I contacted Serbian authorities. I requested data on the census, 1991, 2002. I requested data on the refugees and IDPs within Serbia, and I did exactly the same thing with the Croats. So there is nothing different in these two approaches, and there is nothing about taking sides. I have not taken any sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that you did not have at your disposal official data on property exchanges. However, since these are contracts that are registered properly with courts of law and they are accessible to all interested parties, why didn't you try to get a hold of these contracts? For instance, in Hrtkovci, there were, say, 1.000 Croats living there. Now there are a lot less. You have a census from 1991, and now you see that there are less Croats now and to what extent. You go to the Municipal Court in Ruma and you ask for information regarding their property, and then they give you a survey. Everything is computerised now. The computer provides you this data straight away. I'm not very knowledgeable about computers, but I guess it's like an exhaust pipe: It just gets out. So you see that there is an exchange and some property was exchanged for another property with somebody else. Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: My task was to make a report on out-migration. In the initial stage, it was out-migration from Vojvodina, the province. Later, this task was evolving due to the lack of appropriate data, and we ended with a study of Hrtkovci, but the task was still the same: Migration, out-migration in particular of Croats and non-Serbs. If I had been tasked with a report on exchanges, then that is a different report. These two can be even associated with each other, but you can't claim that I haven't done things for the report on migration. You know, I haven't done things on exchange. It wasn't a report on exchange issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, when you compiled your report, did you know or were you told by the OTP that apartments had been exchanged? Were you aware of that or not, and did you prepare your report by not taking this into account?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was tasked, I was unaware of exchanges of the property between these two groups of the population, and I learned about it in the course of the project. But, still, my task remained exactly the same. From the beginning, it was a task for a demographer, a study of migration. That is, of course, related in some way to property as, say -- I don't know how to say it as a broader context for this migration. But it was not that I was specifically tasked to study both the trends, the patterns, and the causes of the migration. So it was a descriptive study of migration patterns, on the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, are you aware of the fact that a person who regularly, in conformity with all possible regulations, carries out an exchange of property, and after that moves out, such a person cannot be considered a refugee in accordance with the provisions of international law? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, before the witness answers this question, I would suggest that the witness is not in a position to answer this question because she's not a lawyer. Now, your position seems to be that because people voluntarily exchanged their property between Serbia and Croatia, they cannot be refugees in the legal sense, but I don't see any reason why you put together the fact that people exchanged their properties on a voluntary basis, on the one hand, and on the other, that they might do so because they actually felt afraid and felt that they were being threatened and persecuted. You cannot conclude from the fact that people exchanged their properties voluntarily that they did not leave involuntarily, so I think it's a bit unfair to put this question to someone who is not an expert in international law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Harhoff, every day I feel fear as I walk into the courtroom, but I still keep on coming in. There is a difference in the intensity of fear. Some people are afraid of rain. Some people are afraid of the wind. That's fear, too, but it's not the same kind of fear that can lead to that kind of flight that a person becomes a refugee and gets that status, leaving everything behind. The difference in intensity of fear is a difference that shows whether people are so frightened that they flee, leaving their property behind, in order to save themselves and their children; or there is some fear, fear of uncertainty, of incidents, of some undefined danger, and then perhaps it might be better if we exchange our property and left. These are two completely different intensities of fear. There is one fear that leads to one becoming a refugee, and this other fear leads to certain exchanges of populations, but that is not by way of becoming a refugee. My thesis is that not a single Croat from Vojvodina was a refugee in Croatia because none of them left, leaving their property behind. That they felt unpleasant, I can understand that, I can believe that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj, thank you very much for your lecture, but my point was that this is not a question that can be put to the witness who is not an expert in international law.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But that witness is referring to lists of expelled persons, refugees, and so on. That is what she says in her expert report, you see. That's what the problem is. The witness is speaking of certain things that she cannot prove had taken place at all, and that is why I'm bringing into question the entire expert report. If the expert has not mastered these categories, if she cannot prove that there was at least one single Croat who was a refugee from Vojvodina, how can one accept her expert report? May I proceed now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Tabeau, tell me, how would you define expelled, evicted, or deported persons? What is an expelled person, an evicted person?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, I believe my private definition would be that the person feels pushed out by all kinds of factors from the place where the person is residing; pushed out, very strong, pushed-out circumstances. This is how I would define it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Please, I'm not asking for your very own definition here. I'm asking for a legal definition or a demographer definition that you were guided by. It has to be a generally-accepted definition. It cannot be your private definition. In international law, there is a definition of an expelled person. A few days ago, the authorities in Belgrade expelled the Montenegrin ambassador and the Macedonian ambassador. They left in 48 hours to leave Serbia, so they were expelled. Also, if soldiers with rifles come to somebody's door and say, "Off you go," those are people who are expelled; and, usually, they are escorted to the border with an armed escort. It is a tangible force that expelled them, not a feeling that their environment does not accept them. A person's inner feeling cannot turn that person into an expellee. For example, I feel totally unpleasant here. I feel like jumping out of my skin, that's how unpleasant I feel. But I don't consider myself to be an expelled person and I'm not trying to run away or anything. On the contrary, I'm trying to relish the circumstances involved. So give me your definition, the one that you proceeded from, from a scientific point of view.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: Well, the definitions are in the data sources that were used for my report, and "refugee" is a term that is used for the data provided by the Croatian authorities; that is, the so-called refugee table that I used. The term "expelled" is used in the title of the list of 280 families, and this list is read together with the letter and some other materials related to the events in Hrtkovci at that time. It seems to be justified to use this term. I'm just using the term after the sources I collected for this report. I'm not using the term "refugee" or "expelled persons" in relation to the parish records that I also used for my report. At the same time, I do include these records in the integrated list that is available in annex A. And in addition to this, what makes me think that the departures from Hrtkovci were not just, you know, voluntary, economic migration, educational migration, things like that. If you look at the ethnic composition, the change in the ethnic composition between 1991 and 2002, it's really dramatic. I can't think of regular demographic factors or socioeconomic factors that would be -- that are the determinants, the factors behind these kind of changes. So the picture, the broader picture, makes me think that, wait, this is not just a regular educational, economic, whatever other, migration. There were certainly forces that caused these dramatic changes in the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Ms. Tabeau, we'll look at those tables tomorrow, but I would like to warn you that you are a Prosecution expert. You are here to prove and show that a certain crime took place. That crime took place -- and that crime, in the Statute of this Tribunal, is defined as a crime against humanity, and that crime against humanity incorporates and encompasses clear forms of perpetration. One of the forms of perpetration is deportation. So you must know the definition of "deportation" for you to recognise it or not recognise it in practice, and not to have to resort to lists from ill-intentioned Croatian sources which didn't even make an effort to show that it was actually deportation that had taken place. You haven't got a single piece of evidence that even one single instance of deportation from Serbia to Croatia took place, and you have not even a shred of evidence and proof to show that there is -- that there is a single Croat who can be defined as a refugee from Serbia. On the basis of the definition in international law, it was your duty to support the indictment in that respect, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I wouldn't know what was my duty to support the indictment. I was requested to make a report on the out-migration from Hrtkovci, and I was able to collect a number of sources, two of which explicitly mentioned in the name of the data included refugee -- the term "refugee" and "expelled persons." I don't have other evidence as to whether these people were transported in an organised way, buses, whether there were soldiers escorting them, et cetera, et cetera. I don't have this evidence, and I didn't use this in my report. But, still, I believe I made a relevant report which is quite informative and is helpful in a better understanding of what happened in these territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I don't know who might find this useful. It's certainly not in the interests of justice to cloud the issue, to cloud the substance, instead of clarifying the substance of the indictment. You have to show whether there were indeed refugees or not, you have to demonstrate whether there were deported individuals or not. There, you had at your disposal certain methodology. You did not avail yourself of that methodology, you didn't use it. And since you've been working in the OTP for eight years, Ms. Tabeau, what is your salary in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Objection to relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This type of question was already put to another witness. I suppose you're either a P-2, P-3, or P-4 staff. It's very well known. Do you have a specific status or are you a staff member of this Tribunal, a staff member of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a staff member of this Tribunal and the United Nations, and I am P-3, professional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P-3. Very well. She's a P-3. You just need to consult all the relevant documents from the United Nations, and you will have the answer to your question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have anywhere where I can look it up, Mr. President; and when I asked the last expert witness about that, those sources were not accessible to me. Nobody explained to me what P-1, 2 and 3 up to P-5 is and means, so I don't know that; whereas, I should know it. It would be good if I did know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In your country, the country of your origin and now the country that you have been naturalised in, that is, to say, Poland, the former, and Holland, the latter, where an expert appears in court, he can in that capacity testify only if there are absolutely no common points with the prosecution, no points of contact with the prosecution. Is that something you know or aware of?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't understand what are the common points to you. The common point is that my office is in the area of the OTP. But other than that, my office is quite independent; and in the decisions that I make about my work, I'm completely independent. Nobody's telling me how to do things and what -- yeah. I'm an independent expert from this point of view; but, as a matter of fact, the location of the office is the OTP premises in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: However, you do your work as you consider that the Prosecution would like to see you do it, because had you not done it that way, they wouldn't have had you there for eight years, but you would have been dismissed earlier on. So you cannot be an unbiased and international person in the scientific and professional sense; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think it is right. Your comment goes very far. You are saying the Prosecution is telling me what kind of results I'm supposed to produce. I just said I'm independent in my work, and nobody's telling me how to do my work and what kind of results to obtain. The results are obtained from studying the sources, and from data processing, and from studying related materials. This is how we do it. Why do they keep me eight years? You have to ask them that. That is another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why, then, didn't you deal with a serious study, compiling a serious study, but you base your expert report on just three sources: A list of 116 alleged Croats who were refugees, provided to you by unidentified Croatian authorities; and then the parish records; and the book by Marko Kljajic? Those are your three sources, and you have nothing more than that; right? It is on the basis of those three sources that you write your expert report and are presenting yourself and acting as an expert here. It's not very nice to say that you are a Prosecution expert here; whereas, you based your report on just those three sources. It's a bit distasteful.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: What's the question, actually? What do you want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, the question is: Why didn't you compile a serious scientific study on the topic you were given? What you did was allegedly write an expert report on the basis of those three sources and none of them can be reliable in the statistical sense, not a single one of them. Let me make the question simpler. You are a doctor of statistics, as a mathematical method use in social sciences; that's right, isn't it? It was your duty to use a strict methodological principle that your science places at your disposal in order to arrive at scientific truth. On the other side, opposed to that, you used incorrect methods that are untenable in science in order to support something that cannot be supported, and that is this false indictment. Isn't that right, Ms. Tabeau?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU
utterances.text: I don't think it is right; it is all not right. First of all, my study of Hrtkovci is a very serious study. I must say I like it very much, and, well, it's a very good study. This is one thing. And if you criticise the sources, I would very strongly disagree with you. For instance, if I would have used only the parish records, I would feel already very good about this. Parish records is an excellent source that is often used in demography all over the world. Church books last back for centuries. They were for the first time registers of births and christenings and marriages were initiated in England in the 16th century. So using parish records give us a unique opportunity to study demography in historical populations. That is one of the major sources in historical demography, and the study of Hrtkovci is exactly what it is. It is a study of historical demography. And from the point of view of the sources I use, I am very happy with the sources. But if you speak of your serious study, what would it be? Your serious study. I had a different concept as well, an alternative concept for my work, which then at that time was related to the entire province of Vojvodina and to work with census records, individual records, and individual records on refugees and displaced persons both in Croatia and in Serbia. But my attempts failed because I didn't -- I was unable to collect the appropriate sources for this. I don't think Hrtkovci study is less informative or less serious than the Vojvodina study would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tabeau, we'll have to stop here. We have to adjourn at a quarter past 1.00. We'll resume tomorrow, and Mr. Seselj will proceed with his cross-examination. Let me remind you again that you are not to talk about your testimony with the Prosecution. We'll resume our proceedings tomorrow at 8.30. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of October, 2008, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.14 p.m.,
